extraction.name: Visual Question Answering: Datasets, Algorithms, and Future Challenges
extraction.description: A review paper that critically examines the current state of visual question answering in terms of problem formulation, existing datasets, evaluation metrics, algorithms, dataset limitations, and future directions.
extraction.creator: Kushal Kafle and Christopher Kanan
extraction.rai:dataCollection: This paper does not introduce a new dataset; it reviews existing VQA datasets and describes how several of them were created, including manual collection with Amazon Mechanical Turk, automatic generation from captions, and region-specific prompting.
extraction.rai:dataCollectionRawData: The review discusses VQA datasets built from images from sources such as COCO, NYU-DepthV2, Flickr100M/YFCC100M, synthetic cartoon scenes, and shape images.
extraction.rai:dataManipulationProtocol: The paper standardizes naming for parts of The VQA Dataset by referring to the real-image portion as COCO-VQA and the synthetic portion as SYNTH-VQA.
extraction.rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: For the reviewed datasets, preprocessing/manipulation described includes generating QA pairs from captions with an NLP algorithm, breaking longer sentences into smaller chunks, and constructing multiple-choice options from correct, plausible, popular, and random answers.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: The reviewed datasets use both manual and automatic annotation. COCO-VQA used Amazon Mechanical Turk workers to generate questions and a separate pool of workers to answer them, with ten answers per question. Visual Genome used free-form and region-specific question collection. COCO-QA generated QA pairs automatically from captions.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: The paper analyzes annotation disagreement and consensus-based evaluation, noting that COCO-VQA has about 83% inter-human agreement, many subjective or explanatory questions, and cases where opposing answers both receive credit under the evaluation metric.
extraction.rai:annotationsPerItem: 10 answers per question for COCO-VQA; 3 questions per image
extraction.rai:annotatorDemographics: For SYNTH-VQA human cartoon models, variation includes age, gender, and races.
extraction.rai:personalSensitiveInformation: Age, gender, and race are mentioned for synthetic human models in SYNTH-VQA.
extraction.rai:dataSocialImpact: Potential applications include assisting blind and visually impaired individuals, improving human-computer interaction, and image retrieval.
extraction.rai:dataBiases: The paper emphasizes strong language and answer biases in existing VQA datasets. Many questions can be answered without the image, yes/no answers are skewed toward 'yes,' and annotators tend to ask biased or repetitive questions.
extraction.rai:dataLimitations: Current VQA datasets are limited by small size in some cases, restricted scene diversity, grammatical errors from automatic QA generation, subjective and explanatory questions, low inter-human agreement, evaluation difficulties for multi-word answers, and biases that undermine benchmarking.
extraction.rai:dataUseCases: The reviewed VQA datasets are used to train and evaluate VQA systems and benchmarks, including open-ended and multiple-choice evaluation settings.

name.evidence:
Visual Question Answering:
Datasets, Algorithms, and Future Challenges

description.evidence: In this review, we critically examine the current state of VQA in terms of problem formulation, existing datasets, evaluation metrics, and algorithms. In particular, we discuss the limitations of current datasets with regard to their ability to properly train and assess VQA algorithms. We then exhaustively review existing algorithms for VQA. Finally, we discuss possible future directions for VQA and image understanding research.

isLiveDataset.evidence: In this review, we discuss existing datasets and methods for VQA.

rai:dataCollection.evidence: Beginning in 2014, five major datasets for VQA have been publicly released. These datasets enable VQA systems to be trained and evaluated... In the following subsections, we critically review the available datasets. We describe how the datasets were created and discuss their limitations.

rai:dataCollectionType.evidence: In this review, we discuss existing datasets and methods for VQA.

rai:dataCollectionRawData.evidence: With exception of DAQUAR, all of the datasets include images from the Microsoft Common Objects in Context (COCO) dataset [10]... Visual Genome and Visual7W use images from Flickr100M in addition to the COCO images. A portion of The VQA Dataset contains synthetic cartoon imagery... The DAtaset for QUestion Answering on Real-world images (DAQUAR) [30]... based on images from the NYU-DepthV2 Dataset [39].

rai:dataCollectionTimeframe.evidence: Since the release of the first VQA dataset in 2014, additional datasets have been released... As of this article, the main datasets for VQA are DAQUAR [30], COCO-QA [31], The VQA Dataset [32], FM-IQA [33], Visual7W [34], and Visual Genome [35].

rai:dataManipulationProtocol.evidence: A portion of The VQA Dataset contains synthetic cartoon imagery, which we will refer to as SYNTH-VQA. Consistent with other papers [36, 37, 38], the rest of The VQA Dataset will be referred as COCO-VQA, since it contains images from the COCO image dataset.

rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol.evidence: In COCO-QA [31], QA pairs are created for images using an Natural Language Processing (NLP) algorithm that derives them from the COCO image captions... Longer sentences are broken into smaller chunks for ease of processing... The multiple-choice format contains all the same QA pairs, but it also contains 18 different choices that are comprised of The Correct Answer... Plausible Answers... Popular Answers... Random Answers.

rai:dataAnnotationProtocol.evidence: COCO-VQA consists of three questions per image, with ten answers per question. Amazon Mechanical Turk (AMT) workers were employed to generate questions for each image by being asked to 'Stump a smart robot,' and a separate pool of workers were hired to generate the answers to the questions... Visual Genome consists of six types of 'W' questions... Two distinct modes of data collection were used to make the dataset. In the free-form method, annotators were free to ask any question about an image... The creators of Visual Genome combated this by also prompting workers to ask questions about specific image regions... In COCO-QA [31], QA pairs are created for images using an Natural Language Processing (NLP) algorithm that derives them from the COCO image captions.

rai:dataAnnotationPlatform.evidence: Amazon Mechanical Turk (AMT) workers were employed to generate questions for each image by being asked to 'Stump a smart robot,' and a separate pool of workers were hired to generate the answers to the questions.

rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis.evidence: The multiple answers per question are used in the consensus-based evaluation metric for the dataset... These complications are reflected by inter-human agreement on this dataset, which is about 83%... In many other cases, Accuracy VQA leads to multiple correct answers for a question that are in direct opposition to each other. For example, in COCO-VQA more than 13% of the 'yes/no' answers have both 'yes' and 'no' repeated by more than three annotators.

rai:annotationsPerItem.evidence: COCO-VQA consists of three questions per image, with ten answers per question... Each of the questions is then answered by 10 independent annotators.

rai:annotatorDemographics.evidence: The models also span different age, gender, and races to provide variation in appearance.

rai:machineAnnotationTools.evidence: In COCO-QA [31], QA pairs are created for images using an Natural Language Processing (NLP) algorithm that derives them from the COCO image captions.

rai:personalSensitiveInformation.evidence: The models also span different age, gender, and races to provide variation in appearance.

rai:dataSocialImpact.evidence: There are many potential applications for VQA. The most immediate is as an aid to blind and visually impaired individuals, enabling them to get information about images both on the web and in the real world... More generally, VQA could be used to improve human-computer interaction as a natural way to query visual content. A VQA system can also be used for image retrieval, without using image meta-data or tags.

rai:dataBiases.evidence: COCO-VQA has a large variety of questions, but many of them can be accurately answered without using the image due to language biases. Relatively simple image-blind algorithms have achieved 49.6% accuracy on COCO-VQA using the question alone [36]... 'yes/no' answers span about 38% of all questions, and almost 59% of them are answered with 'yes.'... We have repeatedly discussed the problem of bias in existing VQA datasets in this paper.

rai:dataLimitations.evidence: While DAQUAR was a pioneering dataset for VQA, it is too small to successfully train and evaluate more complex models... The biggest shortcoming of COCO-QA is due to flaws in the NLP algorithm... This results in awkwardly phrased questions, with many containing grammatical errors, and others being completely unintelligible... The dataset also contains many subjective, opinion-seeking questions that do not have a single objective answer... Existing VQA benchmarks are not sufficient to evaluate whether an algorithm has 'solved' VQA.

rai:dataUseCases.evidence: These datasets enable VQA systems to be trained and evaluated... VQA has been posed as either an open-ended task, in which an algorithm generates a string to answer a question, or as a multiple-choice question where it picks among choices.
